title: June 1984
hookLine: the Indian army stormed the Harmandir complex during the martyrdom gurpurab of Guru Arjan; the Akal Takht was badly damaged and many pilgrims died

lines: EARLY JUNE: GURU ARJAN'S MARTYRDOM DAY.
cards: Early June, in Amritsar, is hot. In 1984 it was also the time of a gurpurab: the day Sikhs mark the martyrdom of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, who compiled the scripture and was put to death in Lahore.
Families came to the Harmandir Sahib for it. Grandparents. Children.
Villagers who'd saved for the trip. Many of them had nothing to do with politics. They came to bow, to hear kirtan by the water, to eat langar.
And they were inside the complex when the army came.

teach.b: The government ordered the army to remove the armed militants from the complex. The operation was called Blue Star. A curfew was imposed across Punjab, and at the beginning of June the army surrounded the Harmandir Sahib.
After days of firing, on the night of the fifth and sixth of June, troops entered, and tanks were used against the Akal Takht, where Bhindranwale and his fighters had fortified themselves.
The Akal Takht, the seat of Sikh authority founded by Guru Hargobind, was badly damaged. Bhindranwale was killed. So were many soldiers, and many pilgrims caught inside.
How many died is disputed. The government's own count was several hundred militants and civilians, and eighty-three soldiers.

Many Sikhs, and many independent accounts, believe the true number was far higher, in the thousands, and that many of the dead were ordinary worshipers. Other gurdwaras across Punjab were entered at the same time.
For Sikhs in Punjab and far beyond, it was a deep shock: the Harmandir Sahib attacked, on a holy day.
Sikh remembrance at the Akal Takht calls it the third ghallughara, the third great massacre, after the two of the 1700s you learned about earlier. Afterward, the government repaired the Akal Takht.
Sikhs refused that repair, took it down, and rebuilt it with their own hands, through kar seva, voluntary service.
This week ran from starting again, a language kept, a prayer for open doors and a door opened, through a pause and a crisis, to this.
Today, above all, remember the pilgrims.

how: Each June, Sikhs gather at the Akal Takht and in gurdwaras worldwide for Ardas and kirtan in remembrance of those who died in 1984, and many light lamps or hold vigils.

practice: If you have a candle or a small lamp and it's safe, light it; if not, picture one, a small steady flame, standing for the pilgrims who came for a holy day and for everyone who died that June.
You don't need names; just keep your eyes on the flame, or the picture of it, and breathe slowly. If you pray, remember them in your prayer; if you don't, let the flame do the remembering.

wordCard.voice: Ghallughara. A great massacre — what many Sikhs call June 1984, the third, when the army entered the Harmandir complex and the Akal Takht was badly damaged.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ghallughara, a great massacre; many Sikhs call June 1984 the third, after 1746 and 1762.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the pilgrims. Grandparents, children, villagers who came to bow. Day three hundred eight is done.
